items.title: 8.2 Reversible reactions, microscopic events and dynamic equilibrium

source_refs.note: Topic 8.2, printed pages 168-170 (Figure 8.1), with Quick Check 8.1 as the self-check.

blocks.text: When a reversible reaction is at equilibrium it seems static, but at the microscopic level the reaction never stops: reactant molecules keep converting into products while the reverse process happens at the same time. Consider steam and carbon monoxide reacting under suitable conditions, H2O(g) + CO(g) giving H2(g) + CO2(g), starting with equal moles of both reactants. On mixing, macroscopic changes are observed (changes in concentration), and at the microscopic level the maximum number of collisions per second between H2O and CO occurs at the start; bonds in CO and H2O break and new bonds form to give H2 and CO2, so the forward reaction has its maximum rate at the beginning. As H2O and CO are used up, the forward reaction slows. As H2 and CO2 accumulate, the reverse reaction starts; with their rising concentrations more and more collisions per second occur between them, bonds in H2 and CO2 break and bonds in CO and H2O form, so the reverse rate starts low, gradually increases, and finally becomes constant. Eventually both reactions proceed at the same rate: the reaction is in chemical equilibrium and the concentrations of reactants and products are constant, and unless the system is disturbed no further change occurs.

blocks.alt: Graph of concentration against time. A blue curve labelled [CO] or [H2O] starts high and falls; a magenta curve labelled [CO2] or [H2] starts at zero and rises, crossing the blue curve. At a dashed vertical line labelled Equilibrium both curves become flat, the magenta one above the blue one.

blocks.title: State of chemical equilibrium
blocks.text: The state of a reversible reaction at which the composition of the reaction mixture does not change and the forward and reverse rates are equal is the state of chemical equilibrium.

Plots of concentration against time for a reactant A converting to a product B show the possibilities after equilibrium: the concentrations of reactant and product may be equal, or the reactant may be lower or higher than the product, but in every case the concentrations become constant once equilibrium is established. When the concentrations become constant the reaction may seem to have stopped, but at the microscopic level there is intense activity: individual reactant molecules keep reacting and individual product molecules keep combining to go back to reactants, and the rate of the forward process exactly equals the rate of the reverse. It is therefore a dynamic equilibrium: the system is dynamic because molecules are constantly reacting, while the two rates are the same.

blocks.alt: Three graphs of concentration against time for a reactant A (blue, falling) and a product B (magenta, rising), each with a dashed vertical line labelled Equilibrium after which both curves are flat. (a) A and B level off at the same concentration. (b) A levels off below B. (c) A levels off above B.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.1: Plot of concentration vs time (a) Reactant = Product (b) Reactant < Product (c) Reactant > Product (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.1).
